title: APEX: AFS-based Permutation family for Efficiency and eXtensibility (feat. the APEX Suite)
abstract:
ARX-based cryptographic primitives have received considerable attention for their efficient software implementations. For a long time, however, constructing ARX primitives with provable resistance against single-trail differential and linear cryptanalysis remained an open problem. Dinu et al. addressed this problem by introducing the Long Trail Strategy (LTS), the first general design strategy for establishing such bounds for ARX symmetric-key primitives. A remaining challenge in applying LTS is the systematic design and analysis of large-state S-boxes that combine efficient implementation with strong multi-iteration differential and linear bounds. More recently, Yan et al. introduced a general framework for designing and analyzing such S-boxes, with the AFS family serving as a concrete instantiation. Given their excellent multi-iteration security bounds and outstanding software implementation efficiency, AFS boxes offer a viable solution to the core challenging problem in ARX cryptography—systematic design, accurate analysis, and the pursuit of an extreme and compact balance between cryptographic security and implementation performance. We thus argue that the potential of AFS boxes as nonlinear components in LTS-based primitives has long been undervalued. To demonstrate this potential and address the broader design challenge, we use AFS-64 to construct APEX, an efficient and extensible family of cryptographic permutations spanning state widths from 64 to 1536 bits.

We then instantiate APEX in a broad range of symmetric primitives to demonstrate its extensibility and translate the security and implementation advantages of AFS into complete cryptographic designs. These include small-state hash functions and extendable-output functions, authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) schemes, an ultralightweight block cipher, large-state block and tweakable block ciphers, and large-state hash functions based on the Sponge-F mode and designed for China's Next-Generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms program. We derive differential and linear long-trail bounds for the underlying permutations and adapt the long-trail analysis to rate-restricted, same-capacity, and related-tweak settings. Together with analyses of other major attack classes, these results support the selected step counts and the stated security claims.

Optimized implementations on 8-bit AVR, 32-bit ARMv7-M, and x86-64 demonstrate the practical software efficiency of APEX across diverse processor architectures. For 64-byte (resp. 1536-byte) messages, the small-state APEX-HASH functions achieve $1.14\text{--}1.37\times$ (resp. $1.14\text{--}1.17\times$) and $1.15\text{--}1.16\times$ (resp. $1.18\text{--}1.20\times$) the throughput of the corresponding Esch instances on AVR and ARM, respectively. The small-state APEX-AEAD schemes similarly achieve $1.17\text{--}1.48\times$ (resp. $1.14\text{--}1.19\times$) and $1.15\text{--}1.19\times$ (resp. $1.12\text{--}1.15\times$) the throughput of the corresponding Schwaemm instances. For the large-state hash functions targeting the NGCC program, $\mathrm{APEX}_{1536}^{12}\text{-HASH-F-512}$ achieves $2.09\times$ and $2.88\times$ the throughput of the fastest listed SHA3-512 implementations on x86-64 and ARM, respectively, for a 1-MiB message. The higher-security $\mathrm{APEX}_{1536}^{16}\text{-HASH-F-768}$ and $\mathrm{APEX}_{1536}^{20}\text{-HASH-F-1024}$ profiles achieve 6.02 and 11.82 cycles/byte on x86-64, and 123.72 and 239.63 cycles/byte on ARM, respectively. For block-cipher applications, the ultralightweight $\mathrm{APEX}_{64}^{8}\text{-BC-128}$ achieves encryption and decryption speedups of $1.18\text{--}1.21\times$ over CRAX-S across AVR and ARM, while the large-state $\mathrm{APEX}_{256}^{15}\text{-BC-256}$ achieves $1.77\times$ and $1.65\times$ speedups over SATURNIN-256/256 for encryption and decryption on ARM, respectively. The tweakable block cipher $\mathrm{APEX}_{256}^{15}\text{-TBC-256/128}$ achieves $1.38\times$ and $1.39\times$ speedups over TRAX-L for encryption and decryption, respectively. Taken together, these results show that APEX combines extensibility across state sizes and primitive classes with efficient software implementations on markedly different processor architectures.

1 Introduction
Cryptographic primitives based on the ARX (addition–rotation–XOR) paradigm have been extensively studied
because of their software efficiency. By relying primarily on modular addition, bit rotation, and XOR, ARX designs
can be implemented using simple word-level instructions that map naturally to general-purpose processors. This
makes them particularly attractive for software-oriented cryptographic applications.
    The appeal of this approach predates the modern use of the term ARX. Early ARX-like designs, such as TEA [1]
and XTEA [2], proposed by Wheeler and Needham, explored compact software implementations of block ciphers
using modular addition, shifts, and XOR. ARX structures were subsequently adopted in stream ciphers. Salsa20 [3],
proposed by Bernstein for the eSTREAM project, provided a high-speed software-oriented design built entirely from
ARX operations. ChaCha [4], introduced as a variant of Salsa20, improved its diffusion while retaining excellent
software performance. The resulting ChaCha family has since been widely deployed, most notably through ChaCha20-
Poly1305, which combines ChaCha20 [4] with the Poly1305 authenticator [5] in an AEAD construction specified by
the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) in RFC 8439 [6] and adopted by the Internet Engineering Task Force
(IETF) for use in Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) [7], TLS 1.3 [8],
QUIC [9], and Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2)/Internet Protocol Security (IPsec) [10].
    The same implementation advantages have also made ARX structures prominent in lightweight cryptography.
Introduced by the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA), the SPECK family [11] comprises lightweight ARX block
ciphers with a range of block and key sizes designed for efficient software implementation on resource-constrained
platforms. LEA [12] was designed as a high-speed software-oriented ARX block cipher and was subsequently
standardized as Korean Industrial Standard KS X 3246 [13]. More recently, Ballet [14], a lightweight block cipher
based on a simplified Lai–Massey [15] structure and an ARX round function, was selected as one of the final winners
in the block-cipher category of the 2018–2020 Cryptographic Algorithm Design Competition organized by the Chinese
Association for Cryptologic Research (CACR) [16].
    The use of ARX is not limited to block and stream ciphers. ARX operations have also been employed in hash
functions and large-state cryptographic constructions. BLAKE [17], whose compression function uses a ChaCha-
inspired ARX core, advanced to the final round of the SHA-3 competition [18]. Its successor BLAKE2 [19] further
simplified and optimized the design for software implementation and has been widely deployed in cryptographic
libraries. The Skein hash family [20] is built around Threefish, a large-state tweakable block cipher whose MIX
operation combines modular addition, rotation, and XOR. These designs illustrate that the software advantages of
ARX extend naturally from compact ciphers to large-state and tweakable constructions.
    This implementation simplicity, however, does not translate directly into simple security arguments. Carry
propagation in modular addition couples different bit positions, and a large word-oriented ARX component does
not naturally decompose into small S-boxes whose local differential and linear properties can be combined with
lower bounds on the number of active S-boxes, as in the Wide Trail Strategy (WTS) [21]. Consequently, differential
and linear evaluations of ARX designs have historically relied heavily on computer-assisted searches for reduced-
round characteristics. Deriving strong and provable single-trail differential and linear bounds for a complete ARX
construction remains considerably more difficult. The Long Trail Strategy (LTS), introduced by Dinu et al. [22], was
developed to address this difficulty.
    The original LTS paper considered two candidate ARX-boxes, SPECKEY, adapted from the SPECK-32 [11] round
function, and MARX-2, built from the Skein [20] MIX operation. Motivated by SPECKEY’s lower operation count
and better implementation properties, particularly on 16-bit platforms, the authors selected it as the large nonlinear
component and used LTS to construct SPARX, the first lightweight ARX block-cipher family with provable bounds
against single-trail differential and linear cryptanalysis [22]. MARX-2 was later used as the nonlinear component
of LiARX [23], a lightweight block cipher designed according to the same LTS principle. The same general design
idea also appears in the sLiSCP [24] and sLiSCP-light [25] permutation families, whose nonlinear component is a
reduced-round Simeck [26] instance. In particular, sLiSCP-light underlies SPIX [27] and SPOC [28], two candidates in
the Lightweight Cryptography standardization process of the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology
(NIST), both of which advanced to the second round [29].
    Building on the LTS framework, Beierle et al. introduced the compact 64-bit ARX-box Alzette [30] at CRYPTO
2020. Its structure is SPECK-like, but it uses different rotation constants and places the rotations differently. These
changes strengthen its multi-iteration bounds without giving up efficient software implementation. Alzette is used
directly in the CRAX [30] block cipher and the TRAX [30] tweakable block cipher, and it is the nonlinear component of
the SPARKLE [31] permutation family. SPARKLE in turn underlies the Schwaemm [31] family of AEAD schemes and

the Esch [31] family of hash functions. NIST advanced the submission SPARKLE (SCHWAEMM and ESCH) to the final
round of its Lightweight Cryptography standardization process [29]. Although NIST ultimately selected the Ascon
family [32] for standardization, the SPARKLE submission demonstrated highly competitive software performance.
NIST’s final report [33] notes that, in Weatherley’s size-optimized microcontroller benchmarks, SPARKLE achieved
the greatest speedups over ChaCha20-Poly1305 on the 8-bit AVR platform. On the 32-bit ESP32, it was the only
finalist faster than ChaCha20-Poly1305 in all four tested AEAD cases, while on the 32-bit ARM Cortex-M3, SPARKLE
and Xoodyak [34] were the only finalist hash functions faster than BLAKE2s [19].
    In 2023, Fan et al. [35] proposed another 64-bit ARX-based large-state S-box. However, its reported multi-
iteration differential and linear bounds were weaker than those of Alzette, illustrating the difficulty of designing
large ARX-boxes with strong security bounds across multiple iterations.
    Despite these developments, large-state S-boxes for LTS were still designed and analyzed largely on an instance-
by-instance basis. Yan et al. [36] recently proposed a systematic framework for designing and analyzing such S-boxes,
which is not restricted to ARX constructions. The framework is accompanied by a bit-level model for optimal
long-trail decomposition and the SMCS search technique for deriving tighter multi-iteration differential and linear
bounds. Applied to existing ARX designs, these tools improve the known bounds for Alzette and yield tighter bounds
for SPARKLE.
    As one concrete instantiation of this general framework, Yan et al. introduced the ARX-Feistel Structure
(AFS) [36] family of large-state ARX-boxes. The AFS instances combine inexpensive software operations with strong
multi-iteration differential and linear properties.
    Among these instances, AFS-64 is a natural building block for an extensible software-oriented design. It uses only
32-bit modular additions, XORs, and fixed rotations, while providing stronger trail bounds than Alzette. For one
iteration, its maximum expected differential characteristic probability (MEDCP) and maximum expected linear
characteristic correlation (MELCC) are bounded by 2−10 and 2−6 , respectively; the corresponding bounds for Alzette
are 2−6 and 2−2 . Over two iterations, the bounds become 2−37 and 2−20 for AFS-64, versus 2−34 and 2−17 for
Alzette [36].
    We believe that the value of the AFS family for LTS-based design has not yet been fully recognized by
the cryptographic community, and that its usefulness as a building block for efficient symmetric primitives has
consequently been underestimated. In this work, we demonstrate this potential using AFS-64, the 64-bit instance of
the family. Combining AFS-64 with LTS, we construct APEX, an efficient and extensible family of cryptographic
permutations. To demonstrate this extensibility, we use APEX to construct a broad range of symmetric primitives
spanning different applications and security requirements.

Our Contributions
Our contributions are summarized as follows.
• An efficient and extensible family of cryptographic permutations, APEX, is introduced based on the large-state
  ARX-box AFS-64. Guided by the Long Trail Strategy, APEX combines parallel AFS-64 layers with a width-
  extensible sparse diffusion layer and supports state widths from 64 to 1536 bits. Its common structure provides a
  unified foundation for symmetric primitives with different security and performance requirements. The strong
  multi-iteration differential and linear bounds of AFS-64 also provide a concrete basis for analyzing the permutations
  and selecting their step counts.
• A broad range of symmetric primitives is constructed using APEX, demonstrating the extensibility of the
  permutation family across diverse applications. These constructions include small-state hash and extendable-output
  functions, AEAD schemes, an ultralightweight block cipher, large-state block and tweakable block ciphers, and
  large-state hash functions based on the Sponge-F mode [37] and designed for China’s Next-Generation Commercial
  Cryptographic Algorithms program [38]. They cover different state sizes, security levels, and application settings
  while retaining a common underlying design.
• An extensive security analysis of the APEX permutations and their modes of use is provided. A method for
  selecting the round constants of AFS-64 is proposed by combining fixed-key quasidifferential analysis [39] with
  empirical fixed-key differential and linear experiments. Differential and linear long-trail bounds are derived for
  the full permutations, and the corresponding searches are adapted to mode-specific constraints, including rate-
  restricted endpoints, equal-capacity endpoint constraints, and related-tweak differences. The permutations are
  further evaluated against a broad range of other cryptanalytic techniques. Together, these results support the
  round-constant selection, the selected step counts, and the stated security claims.

3.1.2 The AFS-64 ARX-box
AFS (ARX-Feistel Structure) is a family of large-state ARX-based S-boxes introduced in [36]. An AFS-2n instance
operates on a pair of n-bit words and is specified by a configurational sequence, a rotation sequence, and round
constants.
    In this work, we adopt AFS-64, shortly denoted by A, with configurational sequence 11000011 and rotation
sequence (17, 24, 1, 1, 16, 31, 24, 0). Its instantiation with a 32-bit round constant c is denoted by Ac . The instance

Two ingredients of an LTS argument. A sound LTS security argument depends on two central ingredients.
First, the primitive structure must admit a valid long-trail decomposition, and tight multi-iteration differential and
linear bounds for its ARX-box must be established. Second, among all admissible truncated trails, the analysis must
find the optimal long-trail decomposition, namely the one yielding the largest admissible differential probability or

decomposition and removes the laborious prerequisite of manually characterizing the activity patterns admitted by
the linear-layer functions). In APEX, Ac supplies the measured multi-iteration bounds, while the sparse Feistel layer
Lnb determines the admissible decompositions of the multi-branch permutations.

3.2.2 Choice and Properties of AFS-64
A detailed design rationale and security analysis of the AFS family are provided in [36]. Below, we briefly summarize
its most important properties. AFS-64 is constructed from XOR-of-rotation and addition-of-rotation operations,

constraints. Although all constant rotations have essentially the same cost on 32-bit ARM processors, their costs
differ on 8- and 16-bit microcontrollers. The selected rotation sequence therefore also favors efficient implementations
on these smaller platforms.

3.3.3.5 Yoyo Games
Yoyo distinguishers were introduced in [47] to expose insufficient diffusion in the block cipher Skipjack. We also
investigated Yoyo distinguishers experimentally for reduced-step APEXnb s permutations. For b = 128, we found
probability-one truncated Yoyo distinguishers covering 3 steps, but none covering more than 3 steps. For every
supported state size b ≥ 256, we found probability-one truncated Yoyo distinguishers covering 4 steps, but none
covering more than 4 steps. All longest distinguishers found have the same structure. As customary in the description
of a Yoyo game, we use “plaintext” and “ciphertext” for the input and output of the permutation, although APEX
itself is unkeyed:
1. Choose two plaintexts whose difference is confined to one 64-bit branch in the right half.
2. Apply the permutation to both plaintexts to obtain two ciphertexts.
3. Create two new ciphertexts by swapping one 64-bit branch in the left half between the two ciphertexts.
4. Apply the inverse permutation to the two modified ciphertexts.
The experiment yields a truncated Yoyo distinguisher when the two resulting plaintexts again differ in only one
64-bit branch, a property that is not expected to hold with probability one for a random permutation.

3.3.3.7 Symmetry-Based Cryptanalysis
The use of distinct and dense branch constants, together with the addition of different constants before each step,
breaks symmetries within the APEX permutations. For APEX64 , step-dependent round constants play the same role
by breaking symmetry between successive iterations.
Slide attacks [49]. For APEXnb s with b = 64, the use of a different round constant in each step assures that each
step is different. For b ≥ 128, the XOR of the step counter into the second branch before each step also assures that
each step is different. Therefore, classical slide attacks cannot be applied to the APEX permutations.
Rotational cryptanalysis. Due to the extensive use of dense round constants, we expect APEX to be resistant to

3.4 Implementation Considerations
The APEX permutation family is primarily designed for efficient software implementation. Its AFS-64 branches consist
entirely of 32-bit modular additions, XORs, and fixed rotations, which map naturally to general-purpose processors,
particularly 32-bit architectures. The regular branch structure also permits scalable hardware implementations,
although a detailed hardware evaluation is outside the scope of this work. Since the concrete implementation strategy
depends on the state width, step schedule, and surrounding mode, implementation results are presented together with
the corresponding applications in the following sections. We focus primarily on software implementations throughout

this paper. This software-oriented design choice follows the established distinction in lightweight cryptography
between software-efficient and hardware-efficient primitives, as exemplified by SPECK and SIMON, respectively [11].

5.2.1 Choice of Modes
5.2.1.1 Established-mode strategy.
The purpose of these constructions is to demonstrate the use of the APEX permutation family in lightweight hashing
and authenticated encryption. We therefore employ established modes with well-understood security properties

instead of introducing new modes of operation. This choice separates the evaluation of the underlying permutation
from that of the surrounding mode and permits direct comparison with existing permutation-based designs.

next outer state from distinct combinations of the current outer state and message block. This variant of the Beetle
mode further introduces the rate-whitening map Wc,r . Rate whitening is not part of the original Beetle feedback,
but it can be absorbed into the definition of the underlying permutation and is therefore compatible with the Beetle
framework. In sponge-based authenticated encryption, the rate is visible to the adversary, whereas the capacity
remains hidden. If the rate is aligned with the parallel ARX-box layer, the adversary may directly evaluate part of
the permutation. The copied half of the sparse Feistel linear layer may allow this partial evaluation to extend across
portions of two consecutive steps. We therefore XOR Wc,r (SR ) into the rate before every noninitial permutation call.
Consequently, the rate entering the permutation depends on the hidden capacity, so such a partial evaluation first
requires guessing capacity information. Together with the domain-separation constants, these operations separate
associated-data processing, message processing, complete and incomplete final blocks, and finalization. The four
instances therefore share one mode and differ only in the underlying APEX width and step counts, rate, capacity,
and key, nonce, and tag lengths.

5.2.1.4 Position of message injection.
Across the HASH, XOF, and AEAD constructions, absorbed data are assigned to state branches beginning with the
left half. For HASH and XOF, the image of a message block under M3 or M4 is injected into the complete left half.
For AEAD, the rate first contains all branches of the left half. When r > b/2, it is completed with as many branches
from the right half as required. This placement has three advantages. First, the injected branches enter the Feistel
mixing function in the same step, promoting rapid diffusion through the state. Second, after the AFS-64 layer, the left
half is copied to the right half by the linear layer. An injected contribution therefore passes through two consecutive
AFS-64 layers along the copied path, which reduces the attacker’s control over its propagation. Third, immediately
before each subsequent absorption, the left half already contains the output of the preceding Feistel mixing and
consequently depends on contributions from both halves of the state. An attacker seeking a collision or a cancellation
across absorptions must therefore control both the injected difference and these mixed contributions. This makes
backward propagation and the maintenance of a prescribed pattern immediately before injection more difficult.

5.2.3 Choice of Step Numbers
Following the slim-and-big permutation strategy described in [43], our small-state hash, XOF, and AEAD constructions
use two versions of the underlying APEX permutation with different step counts, referred to as the slim and big
versions. The slim version is used in the performance-critical processing of nonfinal message blocks and between
consecutive output blocks, which dominate the throughput for long inputs. The big version is reserved for security-
sensitive positions: initialization, after the final absorbed block, at phase transitions, and during finalization. At
these positions, it initializes the state, separates processing domains, binds the complete absorbed input, or precedes
the extraction of a digest or authentication tag. We therefore use a larger step count at these positions to provide
additional security margin. For each state width, all HASH, XOF, and AEAD profiles use the same pair (nslim , nbig ),
chosen to satisfy the strongest security requirement among the profiles at that width. This keeps bulk processing
efficient while providing additional security margin at initialization, phase transitions, and finalization.

5.3.1.3 Nonce-misuse setting.
The preceding claims do not apply when a nonce is reused. Duplexed-sponge authenticated ciphers can be vulnerable

slim permutations used during absorption are expected to make full-state recovery difficult in practice. Accordingly,
the construction is expected to retain some practical resistance to key-recovery attacks even under nonce reuse.
In addition, unique associated data may provide effective input uniqueness even if the nonce is repeated. These
observations do not form part of our formal security claim. We therefore require a unique nonce for every encryption
under a given key.

5.3.1.4 Known-key attacks.
The near-capacity security bound of Beetle applies in the secret-key setting. If the key is known, a classical meet-in-
the-middle attack on the sponge state reduces collision and preimage security to approximately half the capacity
when the tag is extracted in one step. This birthday-complexity limitation is common to sponge-based modes. We
do not identify an AEAD use case requiring known-key security and make no known-key security claim for the four
AEAD instances.

5.3.3 Attacks on the Modes
The HASH, XOF, and AEAD interfaces restrict the differences and linear masks that an adversary can introduce
and observe. We therefore refine the full-state analysis according to these mode-specific restrictions.

5.3.3.1 Message injection.
For HASH and XOF, each 128-bit message block is mapped by M3 or M4 and injected into the left half of the state.
For AEAD, the adversary controls the rate part of the state. When r > b/2, this part contains the complete left half
and the required number of branches from the right half. Moreover, the final-block domain-separation constant is
injected into the capacity and may introduce an inner-part difference at a phase boundary.

5.3.3.2 Differential attacks.
To analyze the differential security of the sponge-based constructions, we consider vanishing absorbed trails, in
which a nonzero difference is introduced during absorption and subsequently returns to zero. Let Pvan (a) denote
the maximum probability of such a trail spanning a absorption intervals, and let Uns be an upper bound on the
probability of any differential through one ns -step permutation call. If no absorbed difference cancels an existing
state difference, then Pvan (a) ≤ Unas .
    Let κ denote the target security level. Once Un2s < 2−κ , every trail passing through at least two permutation
calls without cancellation already has probability below 2−κ . Hence, a vanishing absorbed trail with probability
greater than 2−κ must use the next absorption to cancel the state difference produced after the preceding absorption.
The first absorbed difference is restricted to the rate. Immediately before the second absorption, the state difference
must again be restricted to the rate so that it can be cancelled by the next absorbed block. Consequently, it is
sufficient to search for rate-to-rate differential trails.

6.2 Design Rationale and Security Analysis
6.2.1 Choice of the Sponge-F Mode
The NGCC evaluation criteria require the prescribed classical security levels while also taking resistance to generic
quantum attacks into account. For a conventional sponge with a d-bit digest, a c-bit capacity, and squeezing rate r′ ,
the generic collision, preimage, and second-preimage security bounds are min{d/2, c/2}, min{d, max{d − r′ , c/2}},
and min{d, c/2} bits, respectively [37, 53]. In particular, meeting the required d-bit second-preimage security already
forces c ≥ 2d. With the state width fixed to b = 1536, this leaves a rate of at most 512 bits for d = 512, no positive
rate for d = 768, and is impossible for d = 1024. A conventional sponge therefore cannot efficiently realize all three
target profiles using APEX1536 .
    We instead employ Sponge with Feed-Forward (Sponge-F), a variant of the sponge construction introduced in [37].
After each permutation call, Sponge-F XORs the capacity part of the permutation input into the corresponding part
of its output. This feed-forward operation mitigates the invertibility-related limitation of the conventional sponge


                                                                         47
and allows all three target profiles to retain a positive rate while meeting the required classical and generic quantum
security levels.

6.2.2 Parameter Selection
The NGCC requirements prescribe digest lengths d ∈ {512, 768, 1024} together with the corresponding classical
and quantum security levels. To keep the three instances structurally uniform and retain a comparatively high
absorption rate under these requirements, they all use the 1536-bit permutation APEXn1536   s
                                                                                               , so that b = 1536, with
an instance-dependent step count ns .
    For Sponge-F with digest length d, capacity c, and ℓ padded message blocks, the classical collision, preimage, and
second-preimage bounds are d/2, d, and min{d, c − log2 ℓ} bits, respectively. The corresponding generic quantum
bounds are d/4, d/2, and min{d/2, (c − log2 ℓ)/2} bits [37]. Since padding is always applied, a message M is processed
in ℓ = ⌊|M |/r⌋ + 1 blocks. The input restriction |M | < 264 gives log2 ℓ ≤ 64. We therefore choose c = d + 64, which
guarantees c − log2 ℓ ≥ d, and set r = b − c = 1536 − d − 64.

7.2 Design Rationale and Security Analysis
7.2.1 Security Claim
We make no security claim against related-key attacks. Related-key security is a separate and stronger notion than
the standard single-key model, since it grants the adversary access to evaluations under keys satisfying specified
relations [68, 69]. The practical relevance of this stronger access model depends on the deployment environment. If


                                                                                            52
resistance to related-key attacks is required, the key schedule can be modified for the intended class of key relations
and the resulting construction analyzed separately. For APEX15    256 -TBC-256/128, we claim 128-bit security in the
related-tweak setting, provided that the total number of plaintext/ciphertext–tweak queries under any fixed key
does not exceed 2128 . The secret key remains fixed and unknown, while the adversary may choose public tweaks
satisfying adversarially specified relations.

7.2.2 APEX864 -BC-128
The ultralightweight block cipher APEX864 -BC-128 is built directly from the APEX64 step function. To reduce
encryption and decryption latency, we follow the schedule-free key-alternation strategy of CRAX-S [30]. The 128-bit
master key is divided into two 64-bit half-keys. The first and second half-keys are used alternately in the even- and
odd-numbered steps, respectively, and the first half-key is also used for final whitening. This arrangement avoids
both expanded-key generation and round-key storage. To further reduce the software cost, the cipher cyclically
uses only the five constants c0 , . . . , c4 . This five-constant cycle is combined with the injected step index to prevent
direct slide repetitions. Since the constants repeat with period five while the two half-keys alternate with period
two, a repeated constant is paired with the opposite half-key in the latter part of the cipher. The step index further
distinguishes the keyed steps.
    Since APEX864 -BC-128 is built directly from the APEX64 core, its security analysis relies on the cryptanalytic
results for APEX64 presented in Section 3.3. The longest distinguisher found in the analyses of that section covers no
more than three complete steps of APEX64 . One APEX64 step reaches full diffusion under the dependency-matrix
criterion, although this is only a weak structural condition, while two steps satisfy the strict avalanche criterion as
shown in Section 3.3.3.6. Full key-to-state diffusion is also achieved after two steps. We therefore choose the step count
using the heuristic rule ns = ⌈2 + 2 + 1.2 · 3⌉ = 8. The first two terms allocate two steps on each side of the three-step
distinguisher core, corresponding to the number of steps required for full key-to-state diffusion. The factor 1.2 adds
a conservative 20% margin to the longest distinguisher found, rounded upward. This gives the final choice ns = 8.

8 Conclusion
Currently, how to systematically design and accurately analyze cryptographic primitives that achieve an extreme and
compact balance between security and implementation performance has become a core challenging problem in the field
of ARX cryptography. In this paper, we have presented APEX, a scalable family of cryptographic permutations built
around the AFS-64 ARX-box. Its uniform step function supports state widths ranging from 64 to 1536 bits, providing
a common foundation for both lightweight and high-throughput symmetric-key designs. Using this family, we specified
small-state hash functions, extendable-output functions, and AEAD schemes, along with an ultralightweight block
cipher, a large-state block cipher, and a large-state tweakable block cipher. We further developed large-state HASH-F
instances tailored to the requirements of the Next-Generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms program.
    The proposed constructions are supported by a unified design rationale and a comprehensive security analysis.
We derived differential and linear long-trail bounds for the unrestricted permutations and adapted the corresponding
searches to mode- and construction-specific constraints, including rate-restricted, same-capacity, and related-tweak
settings. Together with our analyses of other relevant attack vectors, these results justify the selected step counts
and support the claimed security levels.
    Software implementations on 8-bit AVR, 32-bit ARMv7-M, and x86-64 platforms show that APEX can be
implemented efficiently across markedly different architectures. In particular, the hand-optimized assembly and
vectorized implementations demonstrate that the regular AFS-based structure scales from resource-constrained
embedded processors to high-throughput SIMD software on x86-64. Taken together, these results demonstrate the
versatility of APEX as a permutation foundation for a broad range of symmetric primitives.
